The incident was SUP-100432, Falkon Systems, during a peak ingest window on 2026-03-10 (08:45–09:20 PST) in us-west-2 — search returned wrong doc IDs for ~3.2% of queries and audit-log/billing telemetry was missing for a 22-minute interval (inseam://enterprise-rag-bench/.../jira/customer-support/dsid_ef7f1d5cba204b728e1f4d7cddda7daa__SUP-100432-falkon-embed-index-reconciliation-and-auditlog-gap-major-incident.txt).

Suspected cause behind both symptoms: aggressive in-memory batching in the dense-index-service — amplified by a recent change that increased batch size for latency optimization — caused larger transient memory usage. During the surge, a kernel OOM on node gpu-12 killed the indexer pod, and the in-memory batch was lost before it was flushed/durably acked to the audit-log Kafka stream. That single loss produced both wrong vector→id mappings in search results and the missing audit-log sequence ranges (08:46–09:07), breaking billing reconciliation. Contributing factors were autoscaler bin-packing (pods packed onto one node) and no enforced pre-ack flush on indexer restart; remediation included replaying the missing commit ranges, a pinned read-only replica route, and indexer v2.1.3 with reduced batch size and forced flush-on-SIGTERM.

The change was **PR #21807 — "dynamic scratch reuse and fanout-aware kernel selection to reduce peak GPU workspace"** (Maya Chen), in the runtime (`runtime/scratch_manager.{cpp,h}` + `runtime/kernel_selector.cpp`):

**The problem:** The runtime's attention-heavy ops grabbed their own per-op temp/scratch buffers each call. With interleaved short and long requests (mixed sequences), these transient allocations spiked peak workspace — arena tuning and static activation checkpointing only fixed average memory, not worst-case peaks.

**The two-part fix:**
1. **Dynamic scratch reuse** — a runtime scratch allocator with a lock-free free-list per size-class and *lifetime tagging* of short-lived temp regions, so buffers are reused across operators (attention, rotary, layernorm) within the same execution frame instead of being re-allocated per op, cutting fragmentation and repeated allocations.
2. **Fanout-aware kernel selection** — the kernel selector now uses observed per-model Q·K fanout counters to prefer low-memory fused attention kernels over tiled/packed ones when transient memory would spike.

**Results:** On A100-40GB with a 50% seq_len=32 / 50% seq_len=1024 mixed workload, peak workspace dropped 16.8GB → 12.1GB (~28%); high-fanout workloads saw a ~34% transient peak reduction, at a ~2.3% median latency cost for long requests in the worst case.

**Knobs:** `runtime.scratch_reuse.enabled`, `runtime.scratch_reuse.max_frame_scratch`, and `runtime.kernel_selector.fanout_heuristic` (see `redwood-docs/ops/gpu-memory-tuning.md`).

Source: `inseam://enterprise-rag-bench/.../github/dsid_a193f9b7483248ad86c52e684d98a760__pr-21807-dynamic-scratch-fanout-kernel-selection.txt`. Related context (workspace spikes, `REDWOOD_ATTENTION_KERNEL_PREF=memory`, and the global temp-pool proposal) is in the eng-runtime thread `dsid_1bf020e4ff244b418f6dd9eb1679890d__2060001111-intergpu-temp-pooling-workspace-knob.txt`.

This maps directly to SUP-92247 ("Service account impersonation scoping prevents delegated admin operations in private prod," Aurora — HIPAA-regulated, private VPC). The full ticket is at:

`inseam://enterprise-rag-bench/.../dsid_0c8ea3b2a7fd4392b1f480fe5f0c4725__SUP-92247-service-account-impersonation-scoping-prevents-admin-ops.txt`

**What was happening:** The automation used a service account token obtained by exchanging an internal key with the new token-broker, then called `/v1/admin/users` with the `X-Redwood-Impersonate: user:alice@aurora.com` header. It got `403 insufficient_scope`. The same call with the human admin's own token worked, because that token already carried the admin scopes.

**Root cause (three stacked problems after the control-plane upgrade to token-broker v0.8.2):**

1. **Tenant mapping rules not applied** — the token-broker's `aurora-mappings` rule set (which maps service identities to delegated impersonation grants like `admin:impersonate, admin:users`) wasn't being applied after the upgrade, so tokens were issued with only default scopes `service:read service:write` (visible in the broker log: `issued token sub=svc:onboard-runner scope="service:read service:write"`).
2. **Stale broker cache** — the mapping step actually returned the right impersonation grant when replayed with debug flags, but the token-broker's cache served an earlier cached token profile; cache invalidation was tied to last-deploy timestamp and the 2026-03-08 deploy left entries inconsistent (related to INT-4112's missing cache-buster flag).
3. **Stale scope allowlist in identity-proxy** — the proxy strips any scope not in the tenant's `allowed_scope_table`, and Aurora's table was stale, listing only `service:*` scopes — so even correct scopes would have been filtered out.

**Why the human token worked:** it bypassed the service-account exchange/mapping path entirely — no token-broker re-mapping, no service-account scope filtering — so it kept its admin scopes.

**Fix:** coordinated out-of-band config reload of the token-broker (cache invalidation with cache-buster) plus rolling identity-proxy v1.9.3, which adds a check rejecting stale cached scope profiles. Verified tokens then issued with `[admin:impersonate, admin:users]` and impersonation calls returned 200.

Here is the prescribed sequence for the first 60–90 minutes of a major (Sev1/S0-level) outage, drawn from Redwood Inference's incident response docs:

## First 60 minutes

**0–10 minutes — Acknowledge & declare**
- On-call acknowledges the page within 2 minutes, joins the incident bridge (meet.redwood.ai/incident), and posts initial status to #sre-oncall tagging @oncall-lead (SRE Response Playbook).
- Incident Lead confirms the incident and classifies severity; opens the incident channel (#incident-<service>-YYYYMMDD-001) and the incident doc from the template (Briefing Kit).

- Execute mitigations per runbooks — rollbacks, routing changes, capacity surge — as approved by the IC, logging each action in the timeline. If mitigation fails, prepare rollback/failover plans.

**15–90 minutes — Continue containment**
- The Briefing Kit's "Contain & Mitigate" window runs 15–90 minutes: run troubleshooting playbooks, apply approved mitigations, and keep the timeline updated (scribe posts to the incident doc every 15 minutes); status-page updates every 30 minutes minimum.

**From 60 minutes — Restore sprint begins (iterative 30-minute cycles)**
- Restore Lead cycles: hypothesize → test in canary → promote → validate, with continuous verification (synthetic checks, internal smoke tests, latency samples). Promote canary when it shows 0 errors for 30 minutes and p95 within 1.5× baseline; roll back if error rate rises >3× or latency degrades SLOs for 15+ minutes (Rapid Restoration Sprint).

**Confirming service is healthy again**
- Recovery & Verification (90–240 min per the Briefing Kit): validate service health and SLO metrics for **15–30 minutes of stability** (error rate and latency) before declaring recovery; Rapid Restoration adds that metrics must hold baseline for a **24-hour sliding window** for full post-restore verification. Comm Lead then issues the "Resolved" status update, and the IC assigns the postmortem (due within 72 hours).

This maps to ENG-102345, the hosted SSE "client-hang mode" incident tied to the eu-west-1 edge gateway rollout.

**The gateway-side change:** after the 2026-02-14 edge rollout in eu-west-1, the gateway began more aggressive keepalive multiplexing with a 65-second idle threshold. When it triggered an upstream half-close on idle, it did so without a graceful shutdown signal, and the runtime's session finalizer — which had a defensive regression that suppressed the final "done" event if a session was flagged "already committed" — never sent the terminal event. The backend had finished generating, but browsers never got the final event.

The gateway hotfix deployed to canary on 2026-02-27 was to make the gateway send a `session-terminate: graceful` header before performing any half-close, so the runtime could flush the finalizer. That was paired with a runtime patch (2026-03-05) making the finalizer idempotent so it always emits the explicit `event: done` sentinel even when the "committed" flag is present. Together these cut the repro rate on canary and staged rollout proceeded.

Based on the evidence in your data network, here's the specific risk:

**Cross-tenant cache key collision → one customer's memoized response being served to another customer (a data isolation/leakage incident).**

Supporting sources:

1. **Prior trailing-slash canonicalization mismatch** (`inseam://enterprise-rag-bench/.../slack/eng-releases/dsid_f7a6c9c88d8e4c179e9d6448fc5b02c9__1739023456-modelcache-prefix-normalization-backfill.txt`): A preflight parity check caught exactly this class of bug — staging used `"models/llama/v2/weights/"` while prod stripped the slash, so downstream cache keys differed and canary requests returned `ModelCacheLookup NOT_FOUND`. The fix (`canonical_prefix` with `rstrip('/') + '/'`) had to be made idempotent because downstream consumers treated the no-slash form as canonical. The lesson: if the memoization layer and the request-grouping layer canonicalize differently, the same logical request can hash to two different keys — split-brain caching where some callers hit the memoized entry and others recompute (or worse, coalesce into the wrong group).

2. **What happens when it diverges in multi-tenant form** (`.../slack/eng-platform/dsid_730fa9f825134eb79e6a71c6181bda42__1976543210-telemetry-salt-rotation-collision-metrics.txt`): A real incident where 0.028% of cache hits were "attributed to tenant A that actually served responses for tenant B" — cross-tenant cache key reuse. Their key derivation (`sha256(salt || model_hash || prompt_fingerprint)`, with a global salt and 160-bit truncation) lacked tenant scoping, and batching changes co-located different tenants' requests. Mitigations discussed: include `tenant_id` in the HMAC input, remove truncation (256-bit keys), and add collision-detection telemetry + a nightly scan alerting above 0.01%.

3. **Analogous incident** (`.../linear/engineering/dsid_9948af11e87b4fa8bc309c4a4b9d4265__ENG-27356-...txt`): key/alias collisions causing intermittent 403/200 mismatches where Org A credentials intermittently succeeded against Org B resources — i.e., cross-org elevation risk.

**Bottom line:** if the refactor lets one caller's key include the trailing slash and another's strip it, in a shared (single-salt / shared-namespace) cache you get two failure modes: (a) cache misses/coalescing misses for identical requests (perf), and (b) more dangerously, if any normalization is partial or the grouping layer maps differently-slash variants into the same group, requests from different customers can coalesce into one memoized entry and a response computed for tenant A can be served to tenant B — a cross-tenant data isolation bug. The fix pattern your org has already used: single idempotent `canonical_prefix` normalization in the runtime, tenant-scoped key material (e.g., `tenant_id` in the HMAC), full-width keys (no truncation), and a collision-detection/nightly-scan audit hook.

The rule is the **Decision Score (DS)** from the "Probe heatmap → rollout decision protocol" doc (`inseam://...confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/regression-triage/dsid_b4bd83b46612452e858bc02b380082e2__probe-heatmap-rollout-decision-protocol-2024.txt`). It converts a probe-heatmap snapshot (per-slice failure counts, median latency, embedding-drift score) over the last 24 hours into a single 0–100 score that maps directly to GO / CAUTION / HOLD / ROLLBACK for a staged rollout:

**Three sub-scores:**

1. **StabilityScore (SS)** — weighted test-slice failure density, normalized by probe priority:
   `SS = 100 × Σ_p (w_p × failure_count_p / max(1, total_calls_p)) / Σ_p w_p`
   with priority weights like CriticalTenantFlows:10, BillingIntents:8, UXTextGen:3.

2. **LatencyPenalty (LP)** — from median latency vs. SLO:
   `LP = 10 × max(0, (median_latency_ms − latency_slo_ms) / latency_slo_ms)`, clipped at 30 (default SLO: 250 ms).

3. **DriftFactor (DF)** — from embedding/vector drift:
   `DF = 50 × embedding_drift_score` (95th percentile, normalized against a 7-day baseline drift).

**Final score:** `DS = clamp(SS + LP + DF, 0, 100)`

**Action mapping:**
- **DS ≤ 15 → GO** (continue rollout)
- **15 < DS ≤ 35 → CAUTION** (slow down: cap at 10% traffic, targeted human review within 4h)
- **35 < DS ≤ 60 → HOLD** (pause rollout, automated bisect + focused probes)
- **DS > 60 → ROLLBACK** (auto-revert to baseline, open incident)

Two hard gates override the score: any CriticalTenantFlows slice with failure rate >0.5% **and** avg severity ≥3 forces ROLLBACK regardless of DS, and if >10% of probes lack current telemetry the decision is INCONCLUSIVE (human approval required). After a rollback, a 2-hour fast-probe sweep must confirm DS < 20 before the rollout can resume.

Related-but-different docs also exist if you want alternatives: PM-70219 (composite 0–100 quality score with tiered de-escalation, `dsid_a1eec46d...`) and the activation-signal synthesis draft (weighted infra/model/safety/human health score, `dsid_ac35d711...`), but the heatmap-DS protocol is the one that exactly matches your description — recent slice failure patterns + latency + vector drift → 0–100 → proceed/slow/pause/revert.

Based on the engineering records, the recommended short-term customer-side mitigation is:

**Treat missing final event as terminal and fall back to polling the status endpoint.** Specifically:

1. **Client-side silence watchdog:** Treat ~10 seconds of SSE silence as terminal — proactively reconnect. When the final `event: done` sentinel doesn't arrive, don't wait for EOF; instead **poll the chat completion/status endpoint** to retrieve the final state, so the reply tail and completion status are recovered even when the gateway's half-close suppressed the finalization event. Support shipped exactly this patch pattern to ChatFlow for ENG-102345 (inseam://enterprise-rag-bench/.../ENG-102345-hosted-sse-client-hang-mode-diagnostic-and-fix-plan.txt — "treat lack of final sentinel as ephemeral and fallback to polling the status endpoint," and "treat 10s of SSE silence as terminal and reconnect to status endpoint").

2. **Polling/chunked fallback mode:** For corporate proxies/gateways that break streaming (e.g., Bluecoat-style idle teardown, `Connection: close` rewriting), the documented interim workaround is switching to **polling/chunked mode**, which works over most proxies; SDK-side this is the **`STREAM_AUTO_FALLBACK`** flag (experimental, can be enabled per API key) that auto-retries as polling after a streaming failure. If customers can install deps, a keep-alive HTTP agent (`keepAlive: true`) also helps avoid the proxy idle teardown.

The underlying cause per the ticket: gateway idle/keepalive half-close + a runtime finalizer regression that suppresses the `done` sentinel when a session is flagged "already committed," causing truncated tails and duplicate 16–64 token repeats on reconnect. The permanent fix (graceful `session-terminate` header + idempotent finalizer emitting `event: done`) is being canary-rolled out, so the polling-fallback mitigation above is the stopgap until then.

- **Top row (anchor + health):** a "replay anchor" widget (copyable request_id + timestamp, click opens trace), a 30-min request-rate sparkline, p99 vs. baseline delta, and tiny KPI chips (global p95/p99, error rate, req/s, active model variants). Target: single operator assesses an incident in ≤5 minutes with one trace.
- **Middle row (cause candidates — cache vs compute vs model):**
  - **KV-cache warmth heatmap** per tenant cohort (p50/p90 hit_rate; include eviction-rate spikes annotated with rollout windows, plus a per-tenant warmth index 0–100 fed by a synthetic `prefix-warm-check` probe — every 60s for canary tenants, 2m for high-priority, rotating 5m for the rest).
  - **Batching panel:** batch.size distribution scatter vs. latency (catches under-batching/splitting).
  - **Model fallback panel:** `model.fallback.count` + fallback.reason table.
  - Optional latency heatmap binned by token length (0–64 / 65–256 / 257–1024 / >1024) — hot rectangles in the >256 bucket point to client workload changes (from the **signal taxonomy doc**).
- **Bottom row (drill anchors):** three slowest sampled traces near the anchor time, each row linking to the trace viewer with model.variant and tags; sanitized prompt-signature JSON snapshots; recent rollout/config-change timeline.
- Every panel gets a **one-line runbook hint** ("If kvcache.hit_rate drop > 20%, check cache-population jobs") and an **owner**.

## 2. Tiered paging (low-noise)

Two complementary mechanisms exist in your docs:

- **Tiered alert thresholds** (tenant-aware rollout plan): Tier 1 (page) = sustained tenant-weighted SLO violation >10m with absolute p99 >800ms, or cold_start_rate >5% on a high-priority tenant. Tier 2 (Slack only) = transient burn >5 for 5m or cost spike >3x. Auto-mitigation carve-out: if fallback rate >30% but fallback success >95%, don't page — open a ticket.
- **Burn-rate suppression by tier** (ENG-451238, `…dsid_a935523c…tiered-burn-suppression.txt`): a "Trace Inlet" ingest hook emits a `drift_confidence` score (EWMA of percentile deltas + spectral delta, robust to seasonality); paging requires burn-rate **plus** corroborating drift confidence per customer tier (enterprise pages immediately, standard requires drift ≥60 sustained, trial never auto-pages — ticket only). This catches the slow-degrading latency class instant thresholds miss while squelching transient noise. Add a "safety ramp" (2 corroborating signals) and per-cluster circuit-breaker, and measure `suppress_count` / false-suppression during canary.

First-line pager signals from the taxonomy doc: per-model p95 sustained >2x baseline for 5m, kvcache.eviction_rate >10x baseline, batch-size median drop >50%, fallback surge.

## 3. Tracing: hashed prompts + cache hotness, jump-to-trace in minutes

- **Never log raw prompts in spans.** Use a stable `hashed_prompt_sig` attribute (deterministic salted hash) plus `prompt_token_count` — your telemetry contract and privacy-hash bridge PR already establish this pattern. Anchored session_id/tenant_id as first-class annotations.
- **Required span attributes:** `inference.request_id`, `model.variant`, `tenant.id` (hashed), `sequence_length`, `kvcache.hits` (bool/int), `batching.size`, `fallback.reason`, `kvcache.hit=true/false` on a `serve.kvcache.lookup` span, `batching.window.wait_ms`, `kernel.invoke` (gpu id, queue depth), `model.variant.resolve`. Span names ≤32 chars, lowercase dotted.
- **Sampling:** baseline 0.5% probabilistic; adaptive guarantee of 1 trace/min/tenant at >1 req/s; **auto-uplift rules** — 100% sampling for 10m on the affected shard when eviction_rate >5x baseline AND p95 >1.5x baseline; 100% of fallback flows; 100% on p99-baseline violations or quality-regression drops. Cap uplifted full-trace retention at 7 days.
- **Replay fields (≤2KB blob):** request_id, timestamp, model.variant, hashed_prompt_sig, prompt/response length, kvcache.hits, route_decision_tag, tenant.id_hash, optional pointer to sanitized payload in secure bucket.

## 4. The 15-minute resolution loop

Codify it as quickcards (the tenant-aware doc has these nearly verbatim):

1. **0–2 min:** page opens with a pre-filled triage URL (time range + top-3 signal suspects). Check chips: single tenant or platform-wide?
2. **2–5 min:** quantile/heatmap slicing → is it cache (eviction spike, hit_rate drop), batching (size collapse), or fallback (fallback surge)? Click replay anchor → open one trace anchored on session_id; look for `kvcache.hit=false`, long `serve.model.decode`, or cold-start events.
3. **5–10 min:** apply the matched playbook — KV eviction storm → identify noisy client via per-client token-bucket counters, throttle/pin hot keys, review TTL; fallback oscillation → sticky routing + backoff; autoscaler thrash → hysteresis.
4. **10–15 min:** rollback or flag-flip (sampling/weighting/mitigation flags kept trivially flippable), then verify drift score returns to baseline.

## 5. Validation before GA

Acceptance criteria worth adopting: ≤1 noisy alert/24h attributable to misconfig, ≤5-min median time-to-meaningful-trace (measured on the runbook dashboard), <15% query-cost increase, chaos test proving suppression never blocks true P0 paging, and two tabletop drills with oncall before sign-off.

This is a known interaction between iOS background suspension and the Apple HTTP proxy on managed (MDM) networks. Two tickets in the index explain the failure chain:

**What happens step by step** (from SUP-135791, `inseam://.../dsid_a56c6ba5...apple-http-proxy.txt`, and SUP-218374, `inseam://.../dsid_89b473e4...suspend-thaw-metadata-loss.txt`):

1. **Backgrounding suspends the socket.** When the app is backgrounded ~10–90 s, iOS/OS-level socket suspension drops in-flight keepalives/FINs. On corporate Wi-Fi the Apple HTTP/transparent proxy that MDM installs sees the idle connection and probes it.

2. **Proxy coalesces an idle probe with socket migration.** The edge logs show the signature: `partial_close=true reason=idle_probe_coalesce code=SOCKET_MIGRATE` and `late_fin=true`. The proxy coalesces an idle-probe FIN with a subsequent TCP path migration (connection "warm-up"/hand-off by the device path manager), and the edge treats that unusual FIN+probe sequence as a definitive stream close — *before* the serving runtime has flushed its trailing buffered tokens. This shows up as `stalled-flush: true` with ~120 bytes pending in the flush queue. That's your "few seconds of silence."

3. **Resume is accepted, but the tail is gone.** The client SDK reconnects with its resume token and the resume handshake succeeds — but the edge/server worker has already treated the socket tear as completion and freed the terminal metadata/batch (the worker frees terminal metadata if no pending ACKs for >10 s, per the SUP-218374 root-cause note). So the resumed stream never emits the terminal/`[DONE]`-style event, and the final JSON frame arrives truncated — e.g. client log: `received chunk: "{\"choices\": [{\"text\": \"...and finally we recommend\"}\n\n(EOF)"`.

4. **Possible add-on pathologies.** SUP-218374 also notes an off-by-one sequence bug: the RN client increments seq before suspend, sends seq+1 on resume, which can trigger duplicate prefix tokens after fallback reconnects.

**Why it's specific to managed iPhones on corp Wi-Fi:** the Apple HTTP proxy is present only on those managed networks, and it's the component that probes/migrates the idle backgrounded connection; incidence is higher when the client keepalive interval exceeds 20 s.

**Mitigations found in the tickets:**
- Client side: enable WebSocket fallback in the SDK (0/30 truncations in testing), set keepalive to 15 s, disable resume-on-background in favor of a full reconnect, and raise the reassembly timeout (~8 s).
- Server side: a canary flag `defer-terminal-on-coalesced-fin` (edge-proxy PR #1423) that delays terminal-event emission by 250 ms for sessions matching Apple HTTP proxy heuristics dropped truncation from 12% → 0.8%, plus a fix to persist terminal metadata for ~30 s post-flush and accept out-of-order resume with ±1 seq tolerance.

This is the classic **PMTU blackhole** scenario — and your file network documents it almost verbatim.

## What's happening

**The chain of events (SUP-912345, `inseam://enterprise-rag-bench/.../jira/ops-requests/dsid_84a6d354dca5476b85a34c38d4edfa14__SUP-912345-...`):**

1. The customer's transit provider changed its perimeter firewall policy (confirmed 2026-03-11) and began **rate-limiting/dropping ICMP Type 3 Code 4 "Fragmentation Needed"** messages.
2. Large model shard downloads are done as presigned-S3 **range GETs over HTTP/2 multiplexed streams**. TLS + HTTP/2 push large frames, so the client sends full-MSS (1500-byte) segments with **DF=1** (don't fragment).
3. Somewhere along the peered path (TGW/tunnel/encapsulation), the effective path MTU is smaller than 1500. Normally the downstream router sends back ICMP "frag needed" and the sender shrinks MSS and continues. With the provider filtering that ICMP, the message is generated at the edge router but **disappears before reaching the sending VM**.
4. Result: the sender keeps retransmitting the same oversized packet that can never traverse the path. TCP looks "ESTABLISHED" but sequence progression stops — the HTTP/2 stream sits half-open, partial DATA frames delivered, then a stall, then a 30-second timeout. Small requests and handshakes succeed because they fit under the effective MTU; long-lived multiplexed streams with big DATA frames are exactly what exposes it.

## Why lowering packet size fixes it instantly

Setting the worker **MTU to 1400** (or capping TLS record size server-side to ~1200) means packets never exceed the true path MTU, so no ICMP is needed and no packets get blackholed — SRE confirmed streaming resumed immediately under load. (Connection state doesn't matter; the fix is at the IP layer, which is also why in SUP-215678 `inseam://enterprise-rag-bench/.../jira/customer-support/dsid_031197fb9ab34f6fae5ec1ad5ef5000f__SUP-215678-...` toggling a WAN vendor's "DF-preserve" setting made the failure appear/disappear.)

## Durable fixes recommended in the tickets

- Have the transit provider allow ICMP Type 3 Code 4 (provider ticket TP-44821), or enable **MSS clamping** on the customer edge/NAT device.
- Fix IPsec/GRE encapsulation to allow fragmentation before encapsulation.
- Software-side: the artifact-downloader PR #412 added **adaptive chunking** — falls back from 8MB to 1MB ranges when PMTU signals are absent — plus a `force_small_ranges` support override, and a product RFC for auto-reducing TLS record size when PMTU probes fail.

The diagnostic signature to confirm on your side: traceroute --mtu shows the MTU step-down, tcpdump shows DF=1 segments with retransmits but no ICMP reaching the node, and the egress appliance logs "Fragmentation needed" being sent but dropped.

The fix is documented in the eng-runtime Slack thread (`inseam://enterprise-rag-bench/.../slack/dsid_72b2bd3c2a094fdca6d5f3187a752c24__1919002468-kv-prefetch-batch-trigger-block-heuristic.txt`):

**The change:** reduce `prefetch_window` from 6 → 2 and lower `batch_trigger` from 8 → 4, together with enabling `slab_coalesce=true` and `max_reuse_age=3`.

**Why it was needed:** With `prefetch_window: 6`, the runtime pre-allocates KV blocks for lookahead, and combining that with `batch_trigger: 8` coalesced many streams that each allocated ephemeral workspace slices. This caused frequent compaction (14 compaction events), allocator churn, workspace/kernel-alignment invalidation, fast-kernel fallbacks, and repeated OOM spikes (3 OOM events) on long-context (~4096-token) workloads with paged attention.

**Result on the canary run (200 requests):** peak GPU memory down ~12%, compaction events down from 14 to 4, OOMs → 0 — at the cost of slightly increased tail latency (p50 +3ms, p95 +18ms, deemed acceptable).

The root cause is documented in ticket **INT-918273** (`inseam://enterprise-rag-bench/.../dsid_62ff534dc35a425896b265216f94f69a__INT-918273-observability-agent-impersonation-denied-crosscloud-conditional-binding.txt`), which matches your incident exactly — Dedicated fleet collectors losing GCP service-account impersonation via the AWS STS→GCP broker after an IAM cleanup, with missing metrics/traces in us-east/eu-west for ~36 hours.

**What happened:**

1. **Trigger:** An org-level IAM tightening (Terraform module `iam/roles-v2`) added an attribute-based **conditional binding** on `roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator`, restricting `iam.serviceAccounts.getAccessToken` to calls where `resource.name` matches `projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/serviceAccounts/*` exactly.

2. **Failure path:** The observability agents mint credentials via the STS broker (`arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT:role/redwood-sts-broker`), which uses workload identity federation to exchange AWS credentials for GCP impersonation tokens. The federated principal path evaluates `resource.name` differently (plus a `request.auth.aud` mismatch), so the condition **fails only for broker-issued tokens** — hence intermittent behavior depending on which broker instance handled the exchange (some broker instances included extra claims and worked).

3. **Compounding issue:** A related org policy (`iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains` enforcement) denied federated principals unless a `broker_id` attribute was present in the condition — and the broker's token exchange flow didn't include that attribute. Denials surfaced as `Permission iam.serviceAccounts.getAccessToken denied` and `Condition "resource.name.startsWith('projects/_/serviceAccounts/')" not satisfied`.

4. **Mitigation (2026-03-12 03:40 UTC):** Temporarily added an exception in `iam/roles-v2` for the STS broker principal, matching the broker's token attributes; telemetry ingestion resumed within ~15 minutes.

5. **Permanent follow-ups:** update the STS broker to emit `broker_id` and a stable audience claim, add tests validating IAM condition expressions against broker tokens, and create a runbook for rolling out cross-cloud IAM condition changes.

This was already diagnosed and fixed for your fleet — it's ticket INT-356701 in `internal-support` (`dsid_e20c31eb...surface-arm-metric-flip-breaks-wireguard-split-tunnel.txt`). Here's the answer:

**Why it happens** — a two-part interaction that has to occur simultaneously:

1. **AP-side transient VLAN flip:** On your office AP cluster, a sticky-client policy triggers VLAN reassignment during 802.11r reassociation. When devices roam between the 2.4GHz and 5GHz SSIDs, the AP briefly assigns the client to the **guest VLAN (300)** for ~30 seconds (shown in AP controller logs: "assigned VLAN guest (300) due to NDP mismatch") before restoring the corporate VLAN.

2. **Client-side metric flip:** On Surface Pro ARM devices running Windows 22H2 with the **Qualcomm Wi-Fi driver v4.2.0.13**, the NDIS 6.70 driver recalculates the interface metric on every 802.11r handoff — the event log shows `Interface metric changed: old=25 new=2`. The physical Wi-Fi adapter then gets a *lower* metric than the VPN interface, so even though WireGuard stays "connected" (handshakes and transfer counters keep going), the route table sends 10.10.0.0/16 traffic to the wrong gateway (192.168.50.1 on the guest-VLAN interface), where it's dropped by the edge firewall.

A reboot restores things because it resets the metric and re-establishes the corporate VLAN association. Intel x86 devices were unaffected — it's specific to the Qualcomm NICs on ARM Surfaces.

**Fixes already rolled out (March 2026):**
- GPO + PowerShell script setting explicit interface metrics for the corporate SSID and re-asserting the 10.10.0.0/16 routes on network change
- WireGuard client updated to **1.2.3**, which rejects ephemeral route replacements for pinned split-tunnel subnets
- AP sticky-client policy adjusted to stop transient VLAN flips during 802.11r handoffs
- Qualcomm acknowledged the bug (vendor ticket QC-29812) and shipped a beta driver that pins the interface metric; a permanent firmware fix is tracked under follow-up INT-356802

If you're still seeing it, check that your tablet actually received the GPO metric script and the 1.2.3 client — Asha confirmed the previously impacted machines were fixed after rollout.

The mechanism described in your files is a **dual-path checkpoint-and-resume protocol**, best captured in the ENG-159999 ticket ("Stream probe negotiation and idempotent replay for resilient tool-invocation boundaries," `inseam://.../linear/engineering/dsid_76dec52d65134cb7ad9f1cd2d2a663fd__ENG-159999-...txt`), with supporting designs in the PR (`dsid_268eb6ee473245e28821de9202b8de8c__pr-973410-...txt`) and the disconnected-client-handoff PRD (`dsid_f54c46f313074186bf8a1594334d071d__...txt`).

How it works:

- **Server-issued marker:** The server issues *ephemeral checkpoint hints* — frames containing `{checkpoint_id, epoch, last_seq, fingerprint_window}` — every ~512 tokens (tunable via `X-RI-Checkpoint-Interval`), persisted to the request trace store. Checkpoints are emitted only at safe boundaries (end of a JSON object / end of a tool-call output), never mid-toolcall.
- **Explicit client receipt:** On reconnect the client sends back its last-known checkpoint (`last_seq` + `preferred_checkpoint_id`); the server computes the missing sequence range and replies with a `resume_status` of `ok`, `stale`, or `full-replay`, then replays only the missing range.
- **No re-run of tool side effects:** The runtime marks a tool invocation as *tentative* until the chunk carrying its boundary/commit marker is persisted; replay dedupes on `(session_id, epoch, chunk_fingerprint)` and idempotency keys, so committed tool calls are never re-executed.
- **OpenAI-client compatibility:** Legacy SSE consumers that never send the `X-RI-Stream-Proto: 2` handshake header fall back to a compatibility shim using sentinel `ri-compat` event framing with a short-lived resume token in HTTP headers — so existing streaming clients keep working unchanged. Upgraded clients get the version-negotiated path; the PR version of this is the opt-in `X-Redwood-Resume: checkpoint-id=...;token=...` header plus SDK `resume_from_checkpoint` helpers.

In short: server checkpoint hints (the marker) + client-acknowledged resume (the receipt), with a sentinel-event compatibility shim so plain OpenAI-style SSE clients are unaffected.

`inseam://enterprise-rag-bench/Users/greg/aiui/projects/inseam/benchmarks/fixtures/enterprise-rag-bench/documents/github/dsid_d44db962b3ac4581b28904f7dd33a2c8__pr-56378-parallel-tool-returns-reconciliation.txt`

- T+90m: ramp to **100%** if all gates pass, then begin a 24-hour stabilization log

Your notes have this almost fully designed already — here's a structure drawing from two of your notebooks, the **Template Contrapositives Workbench** (`inseam://...dsid_e528bed0...template-contrapositives-workbench.txt`) and the **Shotforge Patchbook** (`inseam://...dsid_d47504...heuristic-shotforge-patchbook.txt`).

## The prompt set (4 examples total)

- **2 positive exemplars** — correct, short, format-compliant.
- **1 contrapositive** — intentionally wrong but *plausible-sounding* (obviously wrong, not noise).
- **1 correction, immediately after** the wrong example — anchoring the fix in position matters: "correction should immediately follow contrapositive so the model learns the contrast."

Critique line on the wrong example: keep it 6–12 tokens, explicit — "Incorrect because: overclaims / changes format / invents a date." Terse critiques beat long rationales. Your draft sample (the email-summary example C: "The product is totally broken" → Why it's bad: overstates severity → corrected summary) is the working pattern.

**Ordering:** contrapositive in the *middle* of the set, not first — start placement made the model overly cautious; middle gave better calibration. Try 2–3 orderings as a variable anyway.

## Experiment matrix

1. Baseline 0-shot
2. Standard few-shot (2 positive)
3. Contrapositive set (2 good + 1 bad + 1 correction, orderings varied)
4. Contrapositive + scaffold preface ("Do not repeat the mistake in the examples below.")
5. **Negative control**: bad example with *no* correction — to test harm vs. benefit (strong negation words in the bad example can flip polarity if uncorrected)

Keep the wrong example from being the longest example in the set, and keep it sanitized of anything disallowed.

## Scale, variables, metrics

- Run **200 probes per condition** across ~6 probe types (under-specified numeric boundaries, policy edges, role confusion — your starter failure probes).
- Vary: exemplar count, correction present y/n, injection position, temperature (0.0 / 0.2 / 0.6 — run temp 0.0 first to find the hallucination floor).
- Track: hallucination/overclaim rate (asserted facts not in input), refusal rate ("I don't know"), semantic accuracy on a labeled subset, style/format compliance, token-cost delta.

Your own logged evidence supports this: FACTC-01 went from 0.46 → 0.31 hallucination rate just by adding one negative-correction shot — and "negative correction is more persuasive than additional neutral refusals."

## Practical notes

- Start with a small/cheap model, warm up with ~20 benign prompts, tag runs with an experiment key (e.g. `cf:contrap-workbench-2025-07`).
- Keep examples in a copy-paste-friendly shotset block; store templates as JSON (your `templating/fewshots/contrap_v1.json` plan) and reuse.
- Don't conflate high refusal rate with failure — sometimes "I don't know" is the win.
- Open questions worth folding into the sweep: 1 vs. 2 contrapositives before diminishing returns; critiques as free text vs. constrained tags (`[bad:overclaim]`).

The closest match to what you're describing is incident **ENG-781234 — "Burst allocation timebase drift during Private→Dedicated switchover causing opaque throttles"** (`inseam://.../linear/engineering/dsid_31059f73d2d2409488178447167534e6__ENG-781234-burst-allocation-timebase-drift-private-dedicated-switchover-incident.txt`).

**What happened:**
- During an automated Private→Dedicated switchover for a large tenant (Acme, 2026-03-10), the **orchestrator and the admission proxies used different epoch/timebase anchors** for burst-ledger reconciliation.
- A follower node with **minor NTP jitter (~120ms clock drift)** changed its local epoch anchor. When the orchestrator applied its snapshot, the proxy validated the customer's burst credits against its **stale timebase**, judged the ledger inconsistent, and failed closed — issuing **429s / "quota_unavailable" / opaque errors** for ~14 minutes until a forced ledger resync at 18:16 UTC.
- There was **no epoch versioning or monotonicity guard** between the components, so a slightly skewed clock caused them to briefly disagree on the time boundary used for quota calculations.

**Mitigations & fix plan (from the same ticket):**
- Hotfix: raised the admission controller's grace window from 2s → 60s during switchover transactions, plus a forced orchestrator→proxy ledger resync.
- Long term: explicit epoch UUID + monotonic counter in ledger snapshots (so proxies detect stale anchors instead of failing closed), admission checks keyed to the orchestrator leader's epoch, switchover handshake ACKs with a safe-apply window, and a chaos test injecting NTP jitter during switchover.

Related corroborating sources:
- **ENG-77890** (lease fencing/idempotent resets) documents the same class of problem — "inconsistent quota reset behavior... when regional failovers, clock skew, or duplicate reset attempts occur," causing "transient over- or under-throttling."
- **ENG-13890** (reserved-capacity window sync) confirms mismatched quota resets across regions from clock skew/out-of-order resets, driving a `reset_epoch` design.
- A separate Slack thread (`dsid_b53b7d49234f48eb8496e15d1a73e6c2__...-token-panel-time-drift.txt`) shows a similar time-skew effect but on the *reporting* side (Console overstating tokens), not enforcement.

So in short: the cause was **split timebase/epoch anchors between the switchover orchestrator and the admission/gatekeeper proxies, amplified by transient clock skew on a follower node** — proxies validated burst quota against a stale time boundary and rejected traffic (bursty 429s/opaque errors) until the ledger was resynced.

Here's a concrete, evidence-backed recipe for your 7-day tamper-evident export — assembled from your own network's docs and prior cases (including EuroBank Holdings, an EU dedicated-tenant regulator audit scheduled 2026-03-20 that mirrors your situation):

## 1. Scope the export window & fields
Query the audit stream for the exact 7-day window with per-event columns:

`GET /v1/audit/exports?tenant=<tenant>&start=<T0>00:00:00Z&end=<T7>23:59:59Z&format=parquet&redaction=include_metadata`

with fields: `event_id, timestamp, actor_id, resource_id, changes, redaction_reason, legal_basis, consent_timestamp` (per the EuroBank precedent, `inseam://...dsid_1ffa3f05e342408382daa57107ec4297__SUP-845327...`). **Critical**: set tenant config `export.include_meta=true` and raise the redaction-engine `rule_lookup_timeout` (the EuroBank case lost `redaction_reason`/`legal_basis` columns when rule lookups timed out, because include_meta was silently inherited as false).

## 2. Per-event masking justification + GDPR tags
- Pseudonymize `actor_id`/`resource_id` with **salted HMAC** (EuroBank's compliance team accepted this, provided the salt fingerprint is documented).
- Emit `redaction_reason` (e.g., `phone_mask`), `legal_basis` (consent / contract / legitimate_interest / legal_obligation), and `consent_timestamp` as separate columns — see `inseam://...dsid_a8201265...__SUP-364501...` (MercuryBank), which used a per-record sensitivity matrix plus `consent_status, legal_basis, data_subject_region, sensitivity_level` and a per-record redaction marker.
- Attach a **redaction mapping document** (field name → rule id → redaction level) so the regulator can see *why* each field was masked.
- Set a manifest flag like `metadata_partial=false` that fails the export rather than delivering events with empty legal-basis metadata (the patch pattern from the EuroBank ticket).

## 3. Tamper-evident packaging
Build the evidence bundle per the admin-provenance bundler spec (`inseam://...dsid_d974507ee1...__ENG-27533...`) and WORM pipeline (`inseam://...dsid_4b5f2a9a78...__ENG-14456...`):
- Deterministic archive (tar.gz or zip of NDJSON/Parquet), with `sequence_number` and `event_received_at` preserved for ordering reconciliation (the Acme case in `SUP-582341` recovered gaps from cold tier — check for sequence gaps before packaging).
- `manifest.json` with canonical SHA256 per file, plus `time_range, region, retention_policy_id, objects[], signature_metadata` (key fingerprint, signer_kid).
- **RFC 3161 trusted timestamp** from your timestamping service over the manifest (both `SUP-582341` and `SUP-71021` confirm this is supported; verify the TSA cert chain).
- **Signed checksum manifest**: sign `manifest.json` with an HSM/KMS-backed key (non-exportable), ship the detached `.sig`. Optionally add a per-batch HMAC using a tenant-scoped KMS key for customer-side validation.
- Optional stronger proof: Merkle root + HSM-signed attestation published to an append-only ledger, so auditors can verify records were in the immutable store at the stated time (ENG-14456).

## 4. Residency & storage
Because this is EU-hosted Dedicated: write the bundle to a **residency-targeted bucket (eu-west) with object-lock/immutability flags**, honoring `data_residency` tags and blocking cross-region copies. Record residency + retention policy id in the manifest.

## 5. Delivery & chain of custody
- Deliver via mutual-TLS SFTP (or signed download URL) and include a written chain-of-custody attestation plus KMS signing attestation screenshot — this is exactly what Acme received in `SUP-582341`.
- Include the verification CLI steps: validate signer_kid, check sha256_manifest, verify RFC 3161 token and KMS signature (`sha256sum` per file; `openssl dgst` for HMAC if used).
- Keep an on-demand export approval workflow logged, and run the verification before the 2026-03-20-style audit date; if exports fail, capture exporter logs + job id for support.

**Key pitfalls from your own history to avoid**: rule-lookup timeouts silently dropping `legal_basis`/`consent_timestamp` columns (SUP-845327); manifests with only a top-level timestamp and no per-file checksums (SUP-364501); sequence gaps from producer retries (SUP-582341). Verify all three explicitly before the regulator sees it.

Based on the eng-runtime canary thread, the change was **hit-aware dynamic windowing of batch formation** (sliding window + kernel-selection bias), which cut the p99/worst-case spikes while p50 stayed flat.

What happened, per the thread (inseam://enterprise-rag-bench/.../eng-runtime/dsid_a5f7f4bc55ca40438e9c1778c866cae8__2234567890-dynamic-windowing-for-prefix-cache-balance.txt):

- **Diagnosis**: When prefix/cache hit fraction hit ~65–80%, the per-batch effective sequence-length distribution became bimodal (many tiny remaining-token runs + a few full-length prompts). During batch formation the kernel selector flipped between `fused_attn_fp16` and the heavier `matmul_fp16` path — an abrupt change in the attention path's per-batch memory/compute profile — driving p99 from ~120ms to ~240ms while p50 stayed steady (~110ms).
- **The fix**: instead of a fixed token budget, a sliding window computes `median_remaining_tokens` and `cache_hit_fraction`; when hit_frac > 0.6 and median remaining length is small, it prefers the fused attention family and tightens `max_batch_len` so batch formation stops migrating to the memory-heavier matmul kernel (config: `dynamic_windowing: enabled`, `hit_aware_threshold: 0.6`, `median_len_threshold: 16`, fused:0.8 / matmul:0.2 family preference).
- **Result (30-min canary on canary-3)**: p99 dropped **240ms → 165ms**, **p50 unchanged (~112ms)**, throughput steady (±2%), kernel-mismatch events down 18% → 4%. Cold/no-cache traffic p99 stayed within 10% of baseline, with ~1.5% throughput cost from more conservative packing.

Related context in your files: the batcher's KV-blindness during admission (token-only budgets ignoring KV footprint) was separately addressed with a `kv_aware_token_clamp` admission policy and soft-trim/deprioritize heuristics (dsid_d428eb19df7a4e1a8ef243523f163790__4087654321-kv-shortfall-batching-policy-checkin.txt and dsid_ecc5d9c99ef946e28c3c4c5dcbb39f44__4850012345-kv-cache-batch-pressure-balancer.txt), and follow-ups proposed making the selector use median+IQR instead of mean and wiring cache_hit_fraction into admission.

This is exactly your incident — **INT-332211: "Access approved but console permissions not provisioned after Okta issuer domain swap"** (`inseam://enterprise-rag-bench/.../jira/ops-requests/dsid_37c24c697d9d462fad0e3afeeea9d8c0__INT-332211-...txt`).

**Root cause:** When the SSO issuer domain was swapped (`okta-old.redwood` → `okta-new.redwood`), access approvals were still being recorded and tokenized under the **old issuer**:

1. The Support Console's approval token generator signs a short-lived JWT whose `iss` claim is whatever Okta issuer is configured at generation time. Approvals queued before the migration (and delivered after) carried `iss=https://okta-old.redwood`.
2. The RBAC grant store indexes grants by **(principal_id, issuer)** — so grants created under the old issuer never matched lookups keyed with the new issuer.
3. The identity-proxy validates tokens against a single expected issuer (`accepted_issuers`), so tokens with the old `iss` were rejected: `ERROR auth: issuer mismatch: token_iss=https://okta-old.redwood, expected=https://okta-new.redwood/oauth2/default`, and console-service logged `RBAC: no matching grants for principal: user:12345 issuer=https://okta-old.redwood`.

So the approval UI showed "Granted" (the approval event itself succeeded), but the provisioning step couldn't translate it into a usable permission because the issuer mismatch broke both token validation and the grant lookup — engineers hitting runbooks/console automation got 403 with "missing RBAC grant."

**How it was fixed:**
- **Short term:** identity-proxy patched to accept both old and new issuers, but only on the access-request/provisioning endpoint.
- **Medium term:** backfill migration job normalized grant keys from the old issuer to the new one for approvals issued in the migration window (2026-03-09 22:00 → 03-10 04:00) — PR `rbac-tools#57`.
- **Long term:** approval tokens now carry an `orig_iss` claim, provisioning canonicalizes the issuer at lookup time, and the retirement playbook gained an explicit migration step for future issuer changes.

Worth noting for your current situation: the team also learned that a 24h grace window on the legacy issuer during the swap wasn't sufficient because token exchange did *not* normalize the issuer as they'd assumed — so check whether your grants created in your migration window need the same backfill.

Here's the step-by-step readiness checklist, assembled from the Frankfurt-region (eu-central-2) bring-up threads in your files — primarily Maya's first-touch runbook and the eu-central-2 bootstrap/handoff runbook discussion.

## Step-by-step bring-up checklist (eu-central-2 / Frankfurt)

**1. Networking & infrastructure preflight**
- Validate VPC/subnets (e.g., control plane 10.120.0.0/19, workers 10.120.32.0/18) and check for CIDR overlap with other regions/prod
- Verify route tables/BGP targets to the central peering fabric, IGW/NAT + egress ranges for image pulls
- Check MTU (WireGuard overlay needs MTU 1420 in the colo; Calico configmap should match, vxlan off) — MTU mismatch has killed large model downloads there before
- Open required ports: TCP 2379–2380 between control-plane nodes, UDP 51820 for WireGuard peers, TCP 10250 from the SRE CIDR for kubelet metrics
- Run an iperf3 test between control-plane and GPU nodes to confirm no fragmentation

**2. Quota checks (the key gating items)**
- GPU quota in the region is soft-capped: eu-central-2 was reported at only **9 available A100s**, so a quota increase request is required before scaling the nodepool beyond baseline (quota ticket took ~48h processing — e.g., ticket #87421)
- Confirm instance-family availability per zone (some zones lacked A100; plan an A10G fallback)
- Also verify vCPU quota for the node flavors and regional IP/alias-IP address headroom — these are common blockers when scaling past the first node
- Open the quota request *before* nodepool scaling, not during

**3. Cluster bootstrap**
- Create control-plane VMs (secure boot off for driver installs); kubeadm init with containerd CRI config
- Pin GPU driver versions and validate kernel ABI before production (DKMS has booted nodes into mismatched kernels)
- Workers join with GPU taints/labels, e.g. `kubectl taint node gpu-worker-01 gpu-node=true:NoSchedule`; for spot/preemptible pool use a spot taint (`node.kubernetes.io/spot: true`) and keep a small reserved baseline — spot for batch, reserved for baseline
- Install base addons: CoreDNS, metrics-server, Calico; install the NVIDIA driver daemonset / device plugin + GFD, then verify

**4. Basic validation**
- `kubectl get nodes` → all Ready
- `kubectl get pods -A` → CoreDNS, calico, metrics-server all Ready
- **GPU usability check:** run a one-off GPU smoke pod running `nvidia-smi` inside a CUDA container (`nvcr.io/nvidia/cuda:11.8.0-cudnn8-runtime-ubuntu20.04`) with `limits: nvidia.com/gpu: 1` — the team's standard smoke pod
- Then a perf smoke test via `kubectl apply -f gpu-smoketest.yaml` + `kubectl logs -f smoketest-pod` (expect >100 tokens/sec on the A100-small baseline), plus LB latency (p50 < 40ms) and KV-cache/NFS mount verification

**5. Acceptance & handoff**
- Acceptance gate: 3/3 nightly perf runs within 10% of baseline and no failed healthchecks for 1 hour
- Hand off with runbook link, escalation contacts (infra oncall, cloud rep), rollback steps (scale down GPU ASG, driver rollback playbook, eu-west-1 fallback)

The rule lives in the **Shadow-to-Solo oncall progression and 24h micro-postmortem toolkit** (`inseam://enterprise-rag-bench/.../confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/dsid_d81e10b32f814357913101ae7579174a__shadow-to-solo-oncall-progression-and-24h-micro-postmortem-toolkit-2026.txt`), Appendix B "when to convert to a full postmortem."

**The rule in short:** A quick, time-boxed **24-hour micro-postmortem** (complete within 24 hours, action items timeboxed to <30 days) is the default fast follow-up for customer-facing latency/availability incidents or incidents triggering rollback/capacity action. You must **convert to the full formal postmortem** — and therefore cannot rely on the quick review — if **any** of these is true:

- Customer **data loss** or **regulatory exposure**
- The incident lasted **more than 4 hours for a SEV1** or **more than 12 hours for a SEV2**
- **Material billing/crediting impact**, or **repeated regressions of the same issue in the last 90 days**

So inverting that: a quick after-action review is acceptable when the incident was short (≤4h at SEV1 / ≤12h at SEV2), didn't cause data loss, regulatory exposure, or material billing impact, and isn't a repeat. On the single-customer-vs-many axis: the severity ladder in the Operational Incident Playbook (`.../confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/dsid_ef0bdaed75c14118bcb85089606161a4__ops-incident-playbook-and-comm-templates-2026.txt`) maps **Sev-3 = single-customer impact / non-critical regression** and **Sev-2 = multiple customers with significant degradation**, and full postmortems are required for Sev-1/Sev-2 (draft in 72h, final within 7 business days). So a quick review is the path for low-severity, single-customer incidents; broad multi-customer impact generally lands at Sev-2+ and triggers the formal analysis.

This is documented in **SUP-672839** ("Accept-queue buildup from ephemeral prewarm handshake triggering sustained 5xx wave") — the Acme Retail dedicated-tenant incident starting 2026-03-12 23:12 UTC in prod:us-east (dedicated capacity pool, redwood-open-7B chat + acme-embedder-v2 embeddings).

**Root cause chain:**

1. **Trigger** — At ~23:10 UTC a high-concurrency burst of long-lived streaming/chat connections arrived simultaneously with Acme's bulk embedding upload job, during peak shopping hours.

2. **Warmup connection churn** — The ephemeral runtime prewarm subsystem responded by spawning warmup workers, each performing multiple short-lived TLS handshakes against the proxy/acceptor. Critically, the autoscaler was concurrently scaling **in** on memory-util thresholds, tearing down warmers while new warmers were spinning up — creating a teardown/spin-up window that amplified handshake churn and SYN backpressure at the acceptor (scale-in events correlated with the start of the staircase).

3. **Accept queue buildup** — The API gateway's accept queue depth rose; `somaxconn`/`net.core.somaxconn` hit defaults on several nodes, new connections saw delayed accepts or early RSTs, and the proxy returned 502/503 with "upstream unavailable."

4. **Disk-backed cache write pressure compounding it** — The serving runtimes' KV-cache was checkpointing to NVMe, producing **write amplification from frequent small writes** → NVMe latency spikes and iowait → delayed worker threads → longer connection hold times → further accept-queue growth, plus runtime evictions/OOM warnings and upstream restarts. This formed the "staircase": each wave of accept failures + slow workers degraded things further, with intermittent short recoveries. (Hypothesis C — NVMe IO saturation from KV-cache snapshotting — had "strong evidence"; gateway threadpool starvation was ruled out.)

**Impact:** ~12% 5xx on streaming chat routes at peak, +400ms p95, truncated messages and reconnect loops; the storefront assistant degraded for several hours.

**Mitigations/fixes:** traffic rerouted to a reserved warm pool (5xx dropped 12% → ~1.8% in 3 min), prewarm concurrency cut 8→2 per node, aggressive KV-cache snapshotting disabled, somaxconn raised (OPS-776). Permanent fixes: autoscaler scale-in policy change (ENG-998), prewarm handshake backoff/connection reuse (RUNTIME-1421), KV-cache snapshot batching with async fsync (RUNTIME-1422), kernel backlog tuning, and a correlating alert on prewarm spawn rate / NVMe iowait / accept-queue depth (MON-312).

Based on the offline bundle format spec (the source of truth for what the installer expects on disk), the bundle MUST extract to a single bundle root containing these mandatory top-level files:

1. **`manifest.json`** — the signed manifest: canonical file inventory (paths, sha256 hashes, sizes, types) plus bundle/release/build metadata. Always required.
2. **`manifest.sig`** — the detached signature over the canonical bytes of `manifest.json`. Required for normal/signed releases; optional only for explicitly approved "break-glass" bundles.
3. **`README.txt`** — the human instructions file: short install instructions, version info, and support pointers. Required.

Optional top-level extras (not mandatory): `manifest.certchain.pem` (embedded cert chain when verification expects it) and an `SBOM/` directory (SBOM may alternatively be referenced externally via the manifest).

- The installer must be pointed at the extracted **bundle root directory**, not the archive — customers may ship a `.tar.zst` but must extract before install.
- Under the root, the required directories are `install/`, `charts/`, `images/`, `artifacts/`, and `config/` (plus the required `images/images.lock`), but the three top-level *files* above are the ones whose presence is mandatory.

I can't generate the actual export artifacts here (I don't have access to the per-call audit records or a signing key), but I can give you the complete tamper-evident proof package specification — including the hardware-backed signed index and local validation steps — modeled directly on how this is done in production at Redwood. Your records doc claims of "nothing lost or reordered" come from completeness + ordering proofs, not trust in the exporter.

## Sources this design is drawn from

- **inseam://…jira/customer-support/dsid_a395cfb9754449c9a12d2037f706807e__SUP-63988-…** — a 72-hour immutable audit batch with tamper-evident index for third-party handoff: NDJSON canonicalization (RFC3339 UTC, LF-only), SHA-256 manifests computed **on raw NDJSON before compression** (a gzip-stage newline bug caused a checksum mismatch on shard 2), a timestamped signed index, chain-of-custody notes, and a short verification guide.
- **inseam://…jira/customer-support/dsid_325127fefd874655adaeb228f5353682__SUP-612984-…** — bank (First Meridian) legal export: ordered event files, per-file SHA-256, ed25519-signed chain-of-custody manifest, **HSM key-rotation attestation bundle** (certs + rotation log showing which key version was active in the window), and a verification runbook with a playback harness.
- **inseam://…linear/engineering/dsid_d3a6c6cda6564a6f8df5f5d137d4ca6f__ENG-35512-…** — the canonical format: JSONL with canonical field ordering, a per-bundle Merkle tree over canonicalized event bytes, Merkle root signed by a **hardware-backed (HSM/KMS sign-only) key**, WORM/object-lock storage, and a verifier CLI that checks hashes, Merkle proofs, signatures, and lock metadata.

## Package layout (3-day window, e.g. 2026-03-01T00:00Z → 2026-03-03T23:59Z)

```
audit-export-2026-03-01__2026-03-03/
├── events/
│   ├── 2026-03-01.ndjson        # per-day shards, canonical JSONL
│   ├── 2026-03-02.ndjson
│   └── 2026-03-03.ndjson
├── manifests/
│   ├── sha256-manifest.txt      # SHA-256 of RAW ndjson (pre-compression)
│   └── merkle-index.json        # per-record leaf hashes → per-day roots → bundle root
├── signed-index.json            # hardware-backed signed index (below)
├── custody/
│   └── chain-of-custody.md      # job ID, operator, generation/packaging/signing/delivery timestamps
├── keys/
│   └── hsm-attestation/         # key version(s) active in window, rotation log, cert chain
└── verify/
    └── verify.sh                # local validation script + guide
```

## Hardware-backed signed index (`signed-index.json`)

```json
{
  "schema": "audit-evidence-index/v1",
  "tenant": "<tenant-id>",
  "window": {"start": "2026-03-01T00:00:00Z", "end": "2026-03-03T23:59:59.999Z"},
  "files": [
    {"name": "events/2026-03-01.ndjson", "sha256": "…", "records": 12345,
     "first_event_id": "…", "last_event_id": "…", "merkle_root": "…"}
  ],
  "bundle_merkle_root": "…",
  "record_count_total": 38702,
  "contiguous_event_ids": true,
  "sequence_gaps": [],
  "canonicalization": {"timestamps": "RFC3339-UTC", "newlines": "LF", "ordering": "event-id,monotonic-seq"},
  "signing_key": {
    "backend": "HSM/KMS sign-only",
    "key_id": "projects/<org>/kms/keys/audit-signing",
    "key_version": "3",
    "attestation": "keys/hsm-attestation/"
  },
  "export_job_id": "audit-export-20260301-01",
  "generated_at": "2026-03-04T02:10:00Z",
  "signature": "<ed25519 or KMS sig-v2 over canonical JSON of the above>"
}
```

**Why this proves "no loss or reorder":** each NDJSON record carries a per-call audit record ID and a monotonic sequence number. The index asserts (a) exact per-day record counts cross-checked against the event source/billing counts (the technique used in SUP-612984), (b) `contiguous_event_ids: true` with an explicit empty gap list, and (c) a Merkle root over the canonicalized bytes — so any omission, insertion, or reordering changes a leaf and breaks the proofs. The signed index is timestamped and signed under the HSM-backed key; the attestation bundle lets the bank independently confirm which hardware key version was active across the whole window (including any rotation).

## Local validation steps for the bank

1. **Checksums:** `sha256sum -c manifests/sha256-manifest.txt` — against raw NDJSON, before any decompression (the SUP-63988 lesson).
2. **Signature:** verify `signed-index.json` signature with the published public key; check the HSM attestation (key version 3, cert chain, rotation log) covers the full window.
3. **Merkle proofs:** run the included `verify.sh` / verifier CLI — recomputes per-record leaf hashes, per-day roots, and the bundle root; compares to `signed-index.json`.
4. **Completeness & ordering:** parse the NDJSON, confirm event IDs are contiguous/monotonic with zero gaps, timestamps fall inside the window, and record count matches the index.
5. **Custody:** review chain-of-custody notes (job ID, operator, generation→signing→delivery timestamps).

Two operational notes worth carrying over from precedent: canonicalize strictly (RFC3339 UTC, LF-only newlines, checksum raw objects before compression — an off-by-one newline at a shard boundary caused a re-sign in one prior delivery), and deliver via single-use, encrypted channel (pre-signed URL or your file-drop bucket with SSE-KMS).

If you'd like, I can also draft the exact `verify.sh` script and the chain-of-custody record template.

This is a known, diagnosed transient issue — retention compaction warmup racing the dashboard read-path. Details from **SUP-835120** (`inseam://enterprise-rag-bench/.../jira/customer-support/dsid_876b1a31bcc7409ab560b9ccbe5a0d41__SUP-835120-historical-panel-staleness-after-retention-compact-warmup.txt`):

**What's happening**
- Scheduled retention **compaction jobs run with `warmup=true`** in us-east. During warmup, partitions are marked compacted while the indexer asynchronously backfills the hot replicas (indexer lag was observed at ~18 minutes).
- Dashboard rollup queries for long time ranges (>30 days) hit a **mix of old and compacted store replicas**; queries landing on compacted-but-not-yet-backfilled partitions return **empty rollups**, and the console frontend renders empty as **zero** instead of falling back to the hot-replica read path.
- The **trace links disappear** because trace anchors are resolved by joining rollup keys to the trace-anchor index, which is being **reindexed during compaction** — when the anchor index is temporarily empty, the UI shows "No traces."
- Everything self-corrects in ~10–30 minutes once the backfill/read-repair completes. **No data loss** — it's purely a read-path consistency problem.

**Symptoms match yours exactly**: >30d panels showing zeroed/stale counts, trace buttons showing "No traces," us-east production, recovers on its own, correlated with compaction windows and indexer backfill events (plus a KV-cache miss-rate spike during warmup).

**Workarounds until the fix rolls out**
- Avoid rapidly toggling wide time windows during scheduled compaction windows.
- Use a time range ≤30 days (reads from hot partitions).
- Admin "Force reload" button forces a hot-replica read.

**Fixes in flight**: frontend treats empty rollup responses as "retry from hot-replica" (console PR #4712), an API fallback read-path, a `warmup-in-progress` header from the indexer (reindexer PR #1189), and an SRE alert for `rollup-empty-during-compaction`.

Based on what I read, the change was **adding hysteresis to the kernel-selection state machine** (i.e., requiring the attention kernel choice to persist for a minimum window/interval before switching back), optionally paired with **eager/pre-loaded kernels and a pooled workspace** so scratch-size oscillation couldn't trigger the switch in the first place.

Evidence:

1. **`inseam://enterprise-rag-bench/.../serving-runtime/dsid_3c725f391b5148f3b92ba3f2a90186a5__adaptive-kernel-degradation-hypotheses.txt`** — In this mixed-length traffic experiment (many short sequences ≤64 interleaved with occasional long ones ≥1024), the runtime flip-flopped between FlashAttention and the paged-attn fallback because transient sequence-length and workspace-shape changes triggered re-selection. The PoC "kernel hysteresis = 5s" forced the kernel choice to persist, cutting **p99 from 230ms → 95ms with throughput flat**; naive workspace pooling (a common pool sized to the max of both kernels, eliminating cudaMalloc churn) improved it further to **~60ms**.

2. **`inseam://enterprise-rag-bench/.../serving-runtime/dsid_9c501b756d8e4feaa27695a14b412414__microburst-queueing-attention-oscillation-case-study.txt`** — The nightly long-context load test showed paged-attn fallback requiring an extra ~96MB workspace allocation plus memcpy (84±12ms switch overhead), producing 356ms p99 blips. The biggest single mitigation measured was **KERNEL_EAGER_LOAD=1** (pre-loading both kernels, removing switch warmup/alloc cost): **p99 356ms → 140ms (~60% reduction)**, and the doc explicitly recommends adding a **kernel-switch cooldown (`min_revert_interval=250ms`)** to stop flip-flop oscillation, noting the long-term fix is "rework kernel selection state machine to be hysteretic and introduce a pooled workspace allocator."

So the answer: the hysteresis/cooldown on kernel switching — preventing the runtime from oscillating into the slower paged-attention path when transient scratch/workspace growth temporarily changed memory and sequence-length signals — gave the largest tail-latency reduction (roughly 2–2.5× p99 improvement), with pooled scratch workspace as the complementary fix that removed the underlying trigger.

That incident matches the **PulseRx** support ticket from **2026-03-11** (SUP-183456), where streaming completions came back with interleaved token sequences and duplicated segments, and billable tokens jumped ~22%.

**Underlying platform cause: a race in the internal streaming multiplexer**, in which per-connection stream IDs could be re-used by the same worker before the KV cache flush completed. The condition was exacerbated during autoscaler scale-up bursts — when new worker PIDs were reassigned, the multiplexer's state machine did not fully quiesce, producing overlapping stream-id windows and replayed token writes (i.e., tokens from concurrent sessions interleaving). The billing spike came from the encoder stage logging duplicated token emissions when handlers retried partial frames.

Evidence cited in the ticket:
- Mux debug log: `"mux: session 0x8a3 collided with 0x9f1 on stream-id 43"` and router events showing `"raced req-id ... timestamp mismatch"` during pool fallback.
- Reproduction required 80+ concurrent short sessions with prefix caching and the default router policy, during a node scale-up in us-east-1.

The fix (PR gh-5501, deployed 2026-03-14) enforced stream-id uniqueness during worker handover in the multiplexer state machine and added an encoder-level dedupe filter to drop repeated token frames mid-stream. Mitigations during the incident included tenant fencing, routing PulseRx to a separate warm pool, and temporarily disabling prefix caching, followed by a provisional billing credit.

There's no single doc for that exact widget, but three design specs together define the requirements for such a panel. Synthesized requirements:

## Requirements for a collapsible tenant sidebar (connectivity + liveness + guarded actions)

**Layout & placement**
- Live as a secondary/docked micro-panel in the existing Private Console nav, built with existing console design-system components and grid (DES-34901, DES-98233).
- Prefer a compact matrix/heatmap as the primary view with expand-to-map for spatial context (matrix-first was chosen for scanability under incident conditions); timeline-first main column with a **collapsible heatmap sidebar** for compactness (DES-98233).
- Limit widget density — prioritize SLO deviations and connectivity over exhaustive metrics (DES-391207).

**Connectivity summary**
- Inter-region matrix showing live status (healthy / degraded / down) per region pair, with colorblind-friendly palette and patterns for degraded states; 3-tier severity badges (OK / Degraded / Critical) mapped to the console palette (DES-34901, DES-98233).
- Per-cluster health plus KV cache status to inform safe rollouts; aggregated route health for selected private clusters.
- Data refresh: default 15s for status overlays, user-configurable, delta updates preferred to save telemetry cost; if metrics are delayed, show last-known snapshot with a freshness timestamp.

**Recent liveness**
- At-a-glance telemetry: cluster-level latency band, node drain status, network path health, recent failover count, inter-region packet loss (DES-391207).

**Top-3 issues**
- The Navigator pattern surfaces the three most important items as the "three safe quick actions" row — each of the top issues pairs with a remediation action (DES-391207). Severity-ranked so on-call users see the critical ones first.

**Guarded remediation actions**
- One-click actions must open a **guarded modal**, create an **audit log entry**, and (DES-391207) carry a **mandatory reviewer approval**, RBAC check indicator before actions enable, plus cooldown badges. Canonical actions: Soft Evict Tenant, Shift Traffic to Failover Region, Start Rolling Drain (safe); also reroute / pause rollout / force rollback. Any interaction that triggers changes requires **multi-step confirmation and 2FA for enterprise tenants** (DES-34901).
- RBAC: non-admins see redacted identifiers and a read-only view; don't expose private IPs or sensitive topology (no BGP/ASN details) in screenshots/exports.

**Estimated failover cost impact**
- Each quick action shows an **inline cost-impact preview** — deliberately coarse (computed in seconds, not exact) so it never blocks the action (DES-391207). The failover simulation should show impacted routes, latency, and estimated cost delta (token throughput delta + approximate per-hour cost impact), with a downloadable impact report/CSV (DES-34901). Include a "why this matters" tooltip explaining cost-delta calculations (DES-98233).

The proposal that matches your description is the **Dynamic Slab Batcher for Streaming Chat** (Linear ticket ENG-11563, `inseam://enterprise-rag-bench/.../linear/engineering/dsid_a84220aa8605488ab48f085ec2da568d__ENG-11563-dynamic-slab-batcher-prefetch-kv-coalesce.txt`).

What it proposes:

- **A small set of preset group ("slab") sizes — 32, 128, and 512 token capacity** — instead of one fixed batch-fill threshold. Incoming streams are assigned to the *smallest slab that fits* the current suffix plus anticipated growth, so tiny chat-style turns batch quickly in small groups while long generations use the large slabs.
- **Latency-budget-driven flushing instead of waiting for full occupancy**: an "early flush window" flushes partially-filled batches at a short watermark (starting at ~6ms) when low-latency SLOs are at risk. The watermark is *dynamically adapted from 6ms up to 40ms based on observed p95 latency vs. the SLO* — i.e., the latency budget decides when to stop waiting, rather than a fixed threshold.
- Supporting elements: sequence-length bucketing to pick the kernel path/slab, KV coalescing across streams sharing prefixes, probabilistic prefetch (capped at ~10–12% of GPU memory), and preemption of small slabs by high-priority interactive streams.

Targeted outcomes in the ticket: p50 token latency ≤18ms for short-turn interactive streams, p95 ≤90ms at 70% utilization, ~25% lower per-stream KV memory, and +18% tokens/sec/GPU for chat with prefix reuse. Prototype results showed ~22% tokens/sec uplift in the perf suite.

The penny drift you're seeing isn't random — it's the exact failure mode documented in several internal billing tickets, and the fix that ended it was three changes to the export/reconciliation path rather than to accounting:

**Root cause (from ENG-374211):** After a mid-cycle plan swap, proration amounts were computed before the final currency conversion, and the conversion used a different rounding strategy than the invoicing pipeline ("usage system uses a spot rate while the invoicing pipeline re-applies a daily rate; the two rounding strategies differ leading to sub-cent drift"). Compounding it, the accounting CSV exporter dropped line items under $0.01, so those tiny corrections "disappear and later be re-emitted by the reconciler as separate correction lines" — which is why your totals come out higher than the processor's export.

**The changes to make:**

1. **Compute proration after final conversion, with one shared rounding policy.** Move the proration calculation to export time, after applying the final invoice-currency conversion, and use a deterministic rounding utility (bankers rounding) shared by both the reconciliation and exporter libraries. Then recompute so "totals reconcile to customer-visible invoice amounts."

2. **Fold sub-cent corrections instead of emitting them.** Implement a `fold_small_correction(invoice_lines, threshold_cents)` step that takes any delta under the threshold and merges it into the nearest non-zero line with the same sign and taxable status, carrying provenance fields (`original_line_id`, `delta_cents`). If folding isn't possible, emit a single corrective line flagged `tiny-proration-correction` — never silently drop it.

3. **Use logical idempotency keys, not run/window keys.** Switch from `<customer>-<hour-window>-<run-id>` to `<customer>-<billing-window>-<logical-invoice-line-hash>` so an updated window *updates* the previously exported line rather than appending a new corrective line. This is what gives you the 1:1 mapping — one exported line per logical charge/credit.

Supporting rules from PM-7311 and PM-4127 worth adopting alongside:
- Do all currency arithmetic in **cents (smallest unit)** and **carry remainders to the most-recent invoice line** to avoid cumulative drift.
- Round platform revenue cents down and track the remainder as a reconciliation ledger entry.
- Export **line-level audit IDs** (e.g., `metering_event_id`) with each invoice line so Finance can match 1:1 against the processor's export.
- Never emit negative invoices for net-negative mid-cycle adjustments — issue a credit memo tied to the original invoice instead.

A backfill note from the engineering ticket: after the flag rolls out, run an offline scan of the last ~90 days for invoices with `proration_delta_abs > $0.50` and auto-merge where folding is safe — that catches the historical drift that's already accumulated.

Found it — this is the BrightHealthAI incident of 2026-03-12, documented in a Confluence postmortem (inseam://enterprise-rag-bench/.../confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/postmortems/dsid_b0b9878c7b11452e9c49e55e4b0b2b11__fallback-routing-to-quant-variant-incident-review.txt).

**What happened:** During the traffic surge (triggered by a customer scheduled-batch misconfiguration), the dedicated pool for BrightHealthAI's **pinned primary model (redwood/rlhf-vicuna-13b)** temporarily exhausted its warm capacity. Smart-routing interpreted this as `capacity_unavailable` and started sending a subset of pinned requests to a "compatible" variant — the legacy quantized model **redwood/quant-13b-q4**.

**Why the fallback bypassed the pin:** The root cause was that smart-routing permitted fallback from a strictly pinned dedicated deployment to a "compatible" variant whenever the pinned pool reported transient capacity exhaustion. The selection algorithm didn't gate on or weight:
- **Warm-pool capability** — the quant variant had no pre-warm pool, so it suffered ~3.2s cold starts
- **Cold-start / throughput risk** — the quant variant had lower throughput, so routing traffic to it converted a short capacity dip into sustained queue growth (>250 pending per worker) and 504s (p95 rose from ~0.9s to ~3.8s; ~7% of requests failed at peak)

Contributing factors: autoscaler didn't pre-warm the quant variant, variant metadata didn't expose warm-pool capability to the router, and the customer's short 200–500ms retry backoff multiplied load.

**Resolution:** A per-customer strict-pinning override (blocking fallback to quant-13b-q4) fixed it within minutes. Post-incident, ENG-3124 added routing guardrails — fallback to legacy quant variants is now disabled by default for dedicated + pinned configurations — and ENG-3140 added telemetry (warm-pool capability, variant selection score, fallback-blocked flag).

This is also consistent with the known gap noted in Linear ticket ENG-31245 ("fallback rules can bypass pinning during capacity events").
